only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.\n> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see\n> [auth/targets](./targets.md).\n\nPassword login is a credential class on the ordinary\n[sessions surface](./sessions-and-principals.md). A successful signin runs the\nsame session-creation core as an email-code exchange and returns the same\ncredential response. There is **no parallel identity system, no parallel token,\nand no separate session shape** — one principal, several credentials.\n\nThis is the first sign-in method a browser app can offer end users without a\nmail adapter. Email-code login still has no self-serve production path (no\ndelivery), so if you need a real user to sign themselves in today, this is it.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.21 -->\n## Declare email identifiers before activation\n\nChoose the password identifier in the app's `defineAuth` program and pass that\nprogram to `defineSchema(..., { auth: { mode: 'sessions' }, authProgram })`.\nUse `identifier: 'email'` for the email-v1 canonicalizer:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/snapback/schema.mjs\nconst authProgram = defineAuth({\n  version: 1,\n  mechanisms: {\n    password: {\n      kind: 'password',\n      identifier: 'email',\n      provider: 'builtIn',\n      recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n    },\n  },\n  assuranceRequirements: {},\n  recoveryPolicy: {\n    recoveryCodes: {\n      enabled: true,\n      requiredWhen: 'no-independent-recovery',\n      rotateAfterUse: true,\n      plaintextCustody: 'one-time-response',\n    },\n    lastAuthenticator: 'enforce',\n  },\n  guestPolicy: { enabled: false },\n  secretReferences: {},\n});\n```\n\nCodegen derives the non-secret `app.authBootstrap` policy from that normalized\nauth program and adds `auth.application-bootstrap.v1` to the generated app's\nrequired capabilities. Do not hand-author either fact. Binding admission\nintersects the generated password mechanism with the target's\n`auth.passwords` capability before credential UI can issue network work. The\nReact template's static acceptance check pins both generated facts:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/acceptance.static.mjs\nassert.equal(descriptor.authBootstrap.format, 'snapback.application-auth-bootstrap.v1');\nassert(descriptor.capabilities.required.includes('auth.application-bootstrap.v1'));\n```\n\n`identifier: 'username'` selects username-v1. An app with no declared password\nmechanism keeps the existing username-v1 default. The choice is stored in\ncatalog v4 at the first sessions activation and is immutable afterward;\ncodegen/startup refuses a later contradictory declaration with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_IDENTIFIER_MODE_IMMUTABLE` instead of reinterpreting\nexisting identities.\n\nThe default password minimum is 12 decoded UTF-8 bytes. To choose a different\napp-wide minimum, set `minimumLength` on the password mechanism:\n\n```js fragment reason=\"policy-only excerpt from the defineAuth password mechanism shown above\"\npassword: {\n  kind: 'password',\n  identifier: 'email',\n  provider: 'builtIn',\n  recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n  minimumLength: 8,\n}\n```\n\nThe declaration is a safe integer from 8 through 128; every password\nmechanism in one program must resolve to the same value or codegen refuses\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_CONFLICT`. The maximum remains 1,024\nUTF-8 bytes, and common-password screening still applies. Omit the field to\nkeep 12. This is a startup policy, so restart the backend after changing it. An\ninvalid declaration refuses codegen/startup with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_INVALID`; an entered password that\nmisses the active policy refuses with `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_POLICY`, whose\nredacted details name the active minimum, maximum, default, and `defineAuth\nmechanisms.<name>.minimumLength` configuration path.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.23 -->\n## Sign up, then sign in\n\n> **One application client owner is one custody context.** In a Node\n> acceptance process, constructing multiple clients without an explicit\n> `storagePartition` can make personas share login: the second client adopts\n> the authenticated durable default owner and can have the same user. Use one\n> stable partition per persona/worker from the\n> [multi-persona client recipe](../recipes/multi-persona-clients.md).\n\nFor an ordinary React application, construct one application client from the\ngenerated `app` and the admitted environment binding, then give that owner to\n`SnapbackProvider`. only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.\n> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see\n> [auth/targets](./targets.md).\n\nPassword login is a credential class on the ordinary\n[sessions surface](./sessions-and-principals.md). A successful signin runs the\nsame session-creation core as an email-code exchange and returns the same\ncredential response. There is **no parallel identity system, no parallel token,\nand no separate session shape** — one principal, several credentials.\n\nThis is the first sign-in method a browser app can offer end users without a\nmail adapter. Email-code login still has no self-serve production path (no\ndelivery), so if you need a real user to sign themselves in today, this is it.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.21 -->\n## Declare email identifiers before activation\n\nChoose the password identifier in the app's `defineAuth` program and pass that\nprogram to `defineSchema(..., { auth: { mode: 'sessions' }, authProgram })`.\nUse `identifier: 'email'` for the email-v1 canonicalizer:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/snapback/schema.mjs\nconst authProgram = defineAuth({\n  version: 1,\n  mechanisms: {\n    password: {\n      kind: 'password',\n      identifier: 'email',\n      provider: 'builtIn',\n      recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n    },\n  },\n  assuranceRequirements: {},\n  recoveryPolicy: {\n    recoveryCodes: {\n      enabled: true,\n      requiredWhen: 'no-independent-recovery',\n      rotateAfterUse: true,\n      plaintextCustody: 'one-time-response',\n    },\n    lastAuthenticator: 'enforce',\n  },\n  guestPolicy: { enabled: false },\n  secretReferences: {},\n});\n```\n\nCodegen derives the non-secret `app.authBootstrap` policy from that normalized\nauth program and adds `auth.application-bootstrap.v1` to the generated app's\nrequired capabilities. Do not hand-author either fact. Binding admission\nintersects the generated password mechanism with the target's\n`auth.passwords` capability before credential UI can issue network work. The\nReact template's static acceptance check pins both generated facts:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/acceptance.static.mjs\nassert.equal(descriptor.authBootstrap.format, 'snapback.application-auth-bootstrap.v1');\nassert(descriptor.capabilities.required.includes('auth.application-bootstrap.v1'));\n```\n\n`identifier: 'username'` selects username-v1. An app with no declared password\nmechanism keeps the existing username-v1 default. The choice is stored in\ncatalog v4 at the first sessions activation and is immutable afterward;\ncodegen/startup refuses a later contradictory declaration with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_IDENTIFIER_MODE_IMMUTABLE` instead of reinterpreting\nexisting identities.\n\nThe default password minimum is 12 decoded UTF-8 bytes. To choose a different\napp-wide minimum, set `minimumLength` on the password mechanism:\n\n```js fragment reason=\"policy-only excerpt from the defineAuth password mechanism shown above\"\npassword: {\n  kind: 'password',\n  identifier: 'email',\n  provider: 'builtIn',\n  recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n  minimumLength: 8,\n}\n```\n\nThe declaration is a safe integer from 8 through 128; every password\nmechanism in one program must resolve to the same value or codegen refuses\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_CONFLICT`. The maximum remains 1,024\nUTF-8 bytes, and common-password screening still applies. Omit the field to\nkeep 12. This is a startup policy, so restart the backend after changing it. An\ninvalid declaration refuses codegen/startup with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_INVALID`; an entered password that\nmisses the active policy refuses with `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_POLICY`, whose\nredacted details name the active minimum, maximum, default, and `defineAuth\nmechanisms.<name>.minimumLength` configuration path.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.23 -->\n## Sign up, then sign in\n\n> **One application client owner is one custody context.** In a Node\n> acceptance process, constructing multiple clients without an explicit\n> `storagePartition` can make personas share login: the second client adopts\n> the authenticated durable default owner and can have the same user. Use one\n> stable partition per persona/worker from the\n> [multi-persona client recipe](../recipes/multi-persona-clients.md).\n\nFor an ordinary React application, construct one application client from the\ngenerated `app` and the admitted environment binding, then give that owner to\n`SnapbackProvider`. The clean browser Explicit fixture is runnable first-party\nsource; its host supplies the admitted binding and platform:\n\n```js source=tests/fixtures/application-auth/browser-explicit/application/App.mjs\nimport React from 'react';\nimport { createSnapbackAppClient } from '@expo/snapback-client';\nimport {\n  SnapbackProvider,\n  useSnapbackAuth,\n  useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal,\n} from '@expo/snapback-react';\n\nimport { app } from './snapback/generated/app.mjs';\nimport { createAuthPanel } from '../../shared/auth-panel.mjs';\n\nconst AuthPanel = createAuthPanel({\n  useAuth: useSnapbackAuth,\n  useCurrentPrincipal: useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal,\n});\n\nexport async function createApplication({ binding, platform, now, onSnapshot }) {\n  const appClient = await createSnapbackAppClient({ app, binding, platform, now });\n  return Object.freeze({\n    app,\n    appClient,\n    element: React.createElement(\n      SnapbackProvider,\n      {\n        appClient,\n        fallback: (state) => React.createElement(\n          'pre',\n          { 'data-fixture': 'boot' },\n          JSON.stringify(state),\n        ),\n      },\n      React.createElement(AuthPanel, { onSnapshot }),\n    ),\n  });\n}\n\nexport { app };\n```\n\n`fallback` owns construction states. When children render, the bootstrap is\n`ready`: binding, custody, client, and authority synchronization have settled.\n`ready` does **not** mean signed in. A cold password-only app still settles a\nserver-witnessed anonymous principal so the entry form is reachable; generated\n`anonymousPublic` controls anonymous app-data access, not whether boot can\nfinish.\n\nInside the provider, use the canonical facade and principal projection. The\ntemplate clears any previous recovery projection before every operation, then\nkeeps the signup result only long enough to render its one-time codes:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/src/App.tsx\nexport function App() {\n  const auth = useSnapbackAuth();\n  const principal = useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal();\n  const workspace = useSnapbackQueries(workspaceQueries);\n  const createTodo = useSnapbackMutation(api.createTodo);\n  const connection = useSnapbackConnection();\n  const [email, setEmail] = useState('person@example.com');\n  const [password, setPassword] = useState('replace-this-password');\n  const [recoveryCodes, setRecoveryCodes] = useState<readonly string[] | null>(null);\n  const todos = workspace.queries.todos.status === 'ready'\n    || workspace.queries.todos.status === 'refreshing'\n    ? workspace.queries.todos.data\n    : [];\n\n  const signUp = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    const result = await auth.signUpWithPassword({ email, password });\n    setRecoveryCodes(result.recoveryCodes);\n  };\n  const signIn = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    await auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });\n  };\n  const signOut = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    await auth.signOut();\n  };\n```\n\nRender all five `CurrentPrincipalSnapshot` states distinctly: `loading`,\n`anonymous`, `authenticated`, `refreshing`, and `blocked`. Only the\n`authenticated` arm has a current `userId`. The template's account UI also\nmakes the recovery handoff explicit:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/src/App.tsx\n        {recoveryCodes ? (\n          <aside>\n            <strong>Save these recovery codes now. They are shown once.</strong>\n            <pre>{recoveryCodes.join('\\n')}</pre>\n          </aside>\n        ) : null}\n```\n\nThe application must hand those codes to the user for separate safe custody\nat signup. They are not session credentials: do not put them in the app\nclient, general persistence, logs, analytics, diagnostics, or a later account\nscreen. Snapback cannot read them back. Clear the projection when the user\nleaves the handoff or starts another auth action. Recovery consumption and\nrotation each return a new one-time set and require the same handling; see\n[Recovery codes are the recovery path](#recovery-codes-are-the-recovery-path).\n\nThe complete ordinary sequence is:\n\n1. Wait for provider `ready`; `useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal()` reports the\n   settled anonymous arm.\n2. Call `auth.signUpWithPassword`. Save the returned recovery codes now; the\n   principal projection becomes `authenticated` only after coordinator\n   adoption and its barrier settle.\n3. On a full browser reload, construct the same app client again. Browser and\n   Expo web use IndexedDB plus Web Locks, so the owner restores the settled\n   principal without another signup or sign-in. `dispose()` only releases the\n   process projection; it does not sign out or delete durable custody.\n4. Call `auth.signOut()`. The provider blanks predecessor protected state,\n   revokes the session, settles anonymous custody, and only then publishes the\n   anonymous principal.\n5. Call `auth.signInWithPassword` for the existing account. Sign-in returns\n   the ordinary credential projection, not recovery codes.\n6. To switch users, sign out first, replace the form identity, then sign in or\n   sign up. Entry while an application-entered or restored principal is still\n   authenticated refuses with a typed `signOut` remediation; there is no\n   implicit latest-user-wins switch.\n\nThe browser restoration path is package-tested against a fresh application\nclient over the same durable custody record:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-client/app-client.test.mjs\n    restored = await createSnapbackAppClient(input);\n    assert.equal(restored.auth.currentPrincipal().status, 'authenticated');\n    assert.equal(\n      restored.auth.currentPrincipal().provider,\n      null,\n      'restoration does not fabricate the provider availability key as issuance provenance',\n    );\n    assert.equal(restored.bootstrapState().authoritySource, 'durable-restored');\n```\n\n### Use the same owner through Expo\n\nAn Expo application passes only the generated `app` to the ordinary provider.\nWhen that descriptor carries the generated bootstrap policy and required\ncapability, `SnapbackExpoProvider` resolves the environment and delegates to\nthe same application-client owner; its `useSnapbackAuth` and\n`useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal` exports project the same contracts. The current\n`expo-chat` template keeps this composition at the root:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/expo-chat/App.tsx\nexport default function App() {\n  const [thread, setThread] = useState<Thread | null>(null);\n  return (\n    <SnapbackExpoProvider app={app} fallback={(state: ExpoBootState) => <BootFallback state={state} />}>\n      <TestPersonaProvider>\n        <AccountEntry />\n        {thread\n          ? <ChatScreen conversationId={thread.id} title={thread.title} onBack={() => setThread(null)} />\n          : <InboxScreen onOpen={(id, title) => setThread({ id, title })} />}\n      </TestPersonaProvider>\n    </SnapbackExpoProvider>\n  );\n}\n```\n\n**Expo web** selects the shipped browser IndexedDB/Web Locks carrier and has\nthe same durable reload restoration as React web. **Both native OS paths ship\nat the exact iOS/Android + `single-runtime` tuples in the published 0.1.24\nclosure** (first publish recorded in\n[the closed custody first-publish gate](repo:issues/closed/20260816-custody-first-publish-gate.md));\nneither path falls back to memory. The iOS receipt proves only the share-sheet extension kind. Its\nbuilt/embedded Notification Service Extension remains a nonclaim because\nsimulator `simctl push` cannot invoke that service stage. The disposable\ncross-platform `expo-chat` template\ntherefore keeps `custody: 'volatile-explicit'`: it can exercise\nsignup/sign-in/sign-out but cannot claim process-death restoration or supported\nrelaunch. Read [Authenticate a native app](./native-apps.md) for the native\nbroker and custody threat boundary, and [Targets](./targets.md) before making\nany hosted or production claim.\n\n### Keep custom identity brokers on the advanced seam\n\nIf the app already has an external identity front door, custom gateway, or\napplication-owned identity binding, keep that explicit composition on the\n[browser sign-in and reload custody recipe](../recipes/browser-auth.md). That\nrecipe deliberately owns a trusted broker, `AuthCoordinator`, and one-use\nexchange; it is not a second spelling for the first-party password journey.\nThe ordinary and advanced owners cannot share one app/storage partition.\n\n### Use the low-level methods only in advanced compositions\n\nThe underlying client methods remain available for custom shells and tests.\n`authPasswordSignup` mints an ordinary session and adopts it into an\napplication-supplied `AuthCoordinator`, exactly as `authExchange` does. You\nneed no admin token, no impersonation capability, and no `auth.mintSession`.\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-client/password-auth.test.mjs\n    const result = await fixture.client.authPasswordSignup({\n      email: 'person@example.com',\n      password: PASSWORD,\n    });\n    assert.equal(result.session.userId, USER);\n    assert.equal(fixture.coordinator.authority.userId, USER);\n    assert.equal(Object.hasOwn(result, 'token'), false);\n```\n\n`authPasswordSignIn` takes the same `{ email, password }` and returns the same\nshape. After either, the client holds an ordinary session: protected queries,\nrefresh, the logout barrier, and reload restoration all behave exactly as they\ndo after an email-code exchange.\n\nBoth methods require an `AuthCoordinator` and an anonymous predecessor — they\ncreate a fresh authority, so they adopt through the same anonymous-issuance\npath `authExchange` uses. The bearer is never returned to your code; the\ncoordinator owns it. An ordinary React or Expo app should not construct that\ncoordinator itself; use the application-client/provider journey above.\n\n## The exact session shape\n\nTwo different shapes carry the user id, at two layers. Both are real; use the\none for the layer you are at.\n\n**On the wire**, `POST /auth/password/signin` returns the LLP 0057 composed\ncredential response — the same five fields as `/auth/exchange`:\n\n```text\n{\n  \"tokenType\": \"Bearer\",\n  \"token\": \"…\",\n  \"refreshAfter\": 604800000,\n  \"session\": {\n    \"id\": \"…\",\n    \"userId\": \"usr_…\",          ← the server-issued principal\n    \"provider\": \"local-password\",\n    \"createdAt\": 0,\n    \"expiresAt\": 0,\n    \"absoluteExpiresAt\": 0\n  },\n  \"authorityDescriptor\": { \"descriptorVersion\": 1, \"authorityInstanceId\": \"aut_…\", \"sessionGeneration\": 1 }\n}\n```\n\n**In the client**, the session projection nests authority, and\n`session.authority.userId` is the principal:\n\n```text\nsession.authority.userId        ← principal id, client-side projection\nsession.authority.isAuthenticated\ncredential.session.userId       ← the same principal, wire response\n```\n\n`session.provider` reports `local-password` at mint **and on every later\nrefresh**, so a session's credential class stays legible for its whole life.\n\nSignup additionally returns `recoveryCodes` — the only response that carries a\nsixth field. Everything else stays byte-shape-identical to `/auth/exchange`.\n\n## Recovery codes are the recovery path\n\nSignup returns eight one-time recovery codes. **They are shown exactly once**\nand are not readable again — not through the admin console, not through any\nroute. Store them at signup or lose them.\n\n- `authRecoveryConsume({ email, code })` mints a session and automatically\n  replaces the whole set. A consumed code cannot be reused.\n- `authRecoveryRotate()` replaces the set for an authenticated principal —\n  use it after suspected disclosure.\n\nRecovery codes never enter coordinator custody, the public credential\nprojection, or error diagnostics.\n\n## Changing a password\n\n`authPasswordChange({ currentPassword, newPassword })` requires both an\nauthenticated session **and** the current password — a stolen bearer alone\ncannot rotate a credential.\n\nChange is a **same-authority rotation**, not a new login: it rotates the acting\nsession's bearer, keeps the authority instance id, and revokes the user's\n*other* sessions. A session belonging to a different user is untouched. Because\nthe authority is preserved, the client adopts it through the same rotation path\nrefresh uses.\n\n`authPasswordSet({ newPassword, stepUp })` adds a first password to a principal\nthat has none. It additionally requires a fresh operation-bound step-up\nchallenge naming the principal's own verified `email-code` identity — acquire it\nwith `POST /auth/request-code` against that address.\n\n## From the CLI\n\nPasswords are accepted on stdin and **never** on the command line, in any\nprofile — so they never reach process listings or shell history.\n\n```sh\nprintf '%s' \"$PASSWORD\" | snapback auth password signup \\\n  --url http://127.0.0.1:4000 --email person@example.com --password-stdin\n\nprintf '%s' \"$PASSWORD\" | snapback auth password signin \\\n  --url http://127.0.0.1:4000 --email person@example.com --password-stdin\n```\n\n`--password-fd N` and the `SNAPBACK_PASSWORD` environment variable are accepted\n**only** under dev and test profiles, and refused elsewhere with a typed code.\n`snapback auth password change` reads the session token first, then the current\nand new passwords, from stdin in that order.\n\nThese verbs need no admin token and no impersonation capability. They are the\nproduct front door, not an operator impersonation path — unlike\n`snapback session mint`.\n\n## What a failed signin tells an attacker: nothing\n\nWrong password, unknown identifier, and locked-out all answer the **same**\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_CREDENTIAL_INVALID` with the same status, body, headers, and\ntiming envelope. A signin against an address with no account still performs a\nfull key-derivation against a dummy hash so the cost is uniform.\n\nLock state is deliberately **invisible on the wire**. A visible lock would\nitself be an oracle: a real account's counter resets when its owner signs in\nwhile a missing address's never does, so lock behavior would diverge across\nhistories and disclose successful-authentication activity. Lock existence,\nthreshold, and expiry are observable only through the authenticated admin\nprojection and `authProgramReadiness`.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.21 -->\nAn operator can call `admin.passwordAttempt(email)`. Its AdminRead response\ncontains the declared `failureThreshold`, `failureWindowMs`, and\n`lockDurationMs`, plus either `attempt: null` or the canonical identifier,\nwindow start, failed count, lock deadline, and current `locked` bit. It never\ncontains the password hash. The corresponding AdminWrite\n`snapback auth password unlock` verb deletes that ledger row early.\n\nDeclared v1 posture — **every threshold is a profile parameter, not a fixed\nconstant**, so acceptance suites and benchmark envelopes can raise them:\n\n| | Default |\n| --- | --- |\n| Consecutive failures before lock | 10 |\n| Lock duration | 15 minutes |\n| Failure window (sub-threshold decay) | 15 minutes |\n| Password length | 12–1024 UTF-8 bytes by default; declare `minimumLength` from 8–128 |\n| Argon2id | m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1 |\n\nAn operator can clear a lock early with the AdminWrite unlock verb; otherwise\nthe lock expires on its own with no intervention.\n\n## Capability boundaries — read before shipping\n\nThese are not shipped, and Snapback says so rather than pretending:\n\n- **Production signup is not blind-accept.** On local/dev/test, signing up with\n  an address that already has an account refuses with a distinguishable code —\n  a deliberate, documented enumeration oracle on the trusted local target.\n  Blind-accept needs mail delivery to notify the real owner, so\n  `authProgramReadiness` reports production signup **unready** rather than\n  faking it.\n- **Mail-delivered password reset does not exist.**\n  `POST /auth/password/reset` works only against the local capture mailbox and\n  refuses outside that profile. Real reset waits on the LLP 0045 mail adapter.\n  Recovery codes are the self-serve path in the meantime.\n- **Reset is same-principal only.** The address's `email-code` identity and its\n  password identity must belong to the same principal. A password-only account,\n  an email-code-only account, and the two-principal squat state all refuse\n  uniformly — transferring a squatter's credential to someone who later proves\n  the address is exactly the hijack this contains.\n- **A password never proves you own the email address.** It proves control of\n  the account whose login name is that string. Only an email-code exchange\n  proves address ownership, and the two claims are separate identity rows in\n  separate provider namespaces. A password identity can never satisfy an\n  email-code lookup.\n- **Catalog v4 is required.** A store created by an older runtime keeps working\n  for everything else and reports the password provider unready — it does not\n  fail. import { app } from '../snapback/generated/app.mjs';
import { AuthBoundary } from '../src/auth-boundary';

if (Platform.OS !== 'web') registerExpoFileSystemRqsFiles(FileSystem, { crypto: Crypto });

function BootFallback({ state }: Readonly<{ state: ExpoBootState }>) {
  const diagnostic = 'diagnostic' in state ? state.diagnostic : null;
  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={styles.fallback}>
      <Text style={styles.title}>{state.status === 'starting' ? 'Opening Clique…' : "Clique couldn't start"}</Text>

    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

  return (
    <SnapbackExpoProvider app={app} fallback={(state: ExpoBootState) => <BootFallback state={state} />}>

    </SnapbackExpoProvider>
  );
}

}

## Candid gaps

- The successful web carrier uses a lane-authored, generated-identity-bound fixed loopback AppBinding/environment for 42000/42001. It is a development-only solution, not a release binding or deployment configuration.
- The schema requests durable-required auth custody. Web persistence is proven by choreography; the optional qualified native custody module is not installed, so the Hermes artifact builds but a native runtime may refuse custody until that carrier is supplied.
- Seeded image/video posts render and suite creation is covered, but the frozen contract has no media-picker compose control, so the app exposes text composition only.
- Backend DM/group/member/receipt operations are implemented, but the frozen M1–M3 UI surfaces do not provide new-DM, new-group, or member-management controls. Choreography retains those limits instead of inferring UI.

// The upload intent is the only door for message images: it names the
// accepted media types, the byte ceiling, delivery, and the strip+variant
// image pipeline. The schema's assetRef field admits only its assets.
export const messageImageUpload = defineAssetUpload({
  args: {},
  auth: 'authenticated',
  accept: { mediaTypes: ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'], maxBytes: 12_000_000 },
  delivery: { kind: 'public-immutable' },
  access: { read: 'via-references' },
  image: {
    location: 'strip',
    variants: [{ key: 'chat', width: 1440, required: true }],

  authorize: async (ctx) => ({ owner: ctx.auth.userId }),

export const sendText = defineMutation({

    conversationId: v.id('conversations'),
    senderId: v.id('users'),
    text: v.string(),

    insert('messages', {
      conversationId: arg('conversationId'),
      senderId: arg('senderId'),
      kind: lit('text'),
      text: arg('text'),
      sentAt: runtimeNow(),
    }, { bindIdAs: 'messageId' }),
    patch('conversations', arg('conversationId'), {
      lastPreview: arg('text'),
      updatedAt: runtimeNow(),
    }),
  ],
  result: results.value(v.object({ messageId: v.id('messages') })),
  returns: returnExpr(record({ messageId: bindingRef('messageId') })),
});

export const sendReply = defineMutation({

    senderId: v.id('users'),

  auth: 'authenticated',
  plan: [

      senderId: arg('senderId'),
      kind: lit('text'),
      text: arg('text'),
      replyToId: arg('replyToId'),

  returns: returnExpr(record({ removed: lit(true) })),

export const sendMessage = defineJsMutation({
  args: {
    conversationId: v.id('conversations'),
    senderId: v.id('users'),
    body: v.optional(v.string()),
    image: v.optional(v.assetRef({ upload: 'messageImageUpload' })),
    replyToId: v.optional(v.id('messages')),
  },
  auth: 'authenticated',
  writes: ['messages', 'conversations'],
  result: results.value(v.id('messages')),
  handler: async (ctx, args) => {
    const hasImage = typeof args.image === 'string';
    const messageId = await ctx.db.insert('messages', {
      conversationId: args.conversationId,
      senderId: args.senderId,
      kind: hasImage ? 'image' : 'text',
      ...(args.body ? { text: args.body } : {}),
      ...(args.replyToId ? { replyToId: args.replyToId } : {}),
      ...(hasImage ? {
        // Admission, message write, and reverse-reference commit are one
        // mutation: attach() is the sole boundary where a finalized upload
        // becomes an application row reference.
        image: await ctx.assets.attach(args.image, { upload: 'messageImageUpload' }),
      } : {}),
      sentAt: ctx.runtime.now(),
    });
    await ctx.db.patch('conversations', args.conversationId, {
      lastPreview: hasImage
        ? (args.body ? `Photo · ${args.body}` : 'Photo')
        : (args.body ?? ''),
      updatedAt: ctx.runtime.now(),
    });
    return messageId;
  },
});

// client call uploads through the intent, then commits the message that
// references the finalized asset. Text-only sends skip the upload phase.
export const send = defineCommand({
  mutation: sendMessage,
  assets: {
    image: {
      intent: messageImageUpload,
      optional: true,
      mutationArg: 'image',

function AccountEntry() {
  const auth = useSnapbackAuth();
  const principal = useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal();
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('person@example.com');
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('replace-this-password');
  const [recoveryCodes, setRecoveryCodes] = useState<readonly string[] | null>(null);

  const signUp = async () => {
    setRecoveryCodes(null);
    const result = await auth.signUpWithPassword({ email, password });
    setRecoveryCodes(result.recoveryCodes);
  };
  const signIn = async () => {
    setRecoveryCodes(null);
    await auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });
  };
  const signOut = async () => {
    setRecoveryCodes(null);
    await auth.signOut();
  };

  return (
    <View style={styles.accountCard}>
      <Text style={styles.accountTitle}>Account</Text>
      <Text style={styles.status}>
        {principal.status === 'authenticated'
          ? `Signed in as ${principal.userId}`
          : principal.status === 'anonymous'
            ? 'Ready to sign up or sign in'
            : `Authentication: ${principal.status}`}
      </Text>
      {principal.status === 'anonymous' ? (
        <>
          <TextInput
            accessibilityLabel="Email"
            autoCapitalize="none"
            autoComplete="email"
            keyboardType="email-address"
            onChangeText={setEmail}
            placeholder="Email"
            style={styles.input}
            value={email}
          />
          <TextInput
            accessibilityLabel="Password"
            autoCapitalize="none"
            autoComplete="current-password"
            onChangeText={setPassword}
            placeholder="Password"
            secureTextEntry
            style={styles.input}
            value={password}
          />
          <View style={styles.accountActions}>
            <Button title="Sign up" onPress={() => void signUp()} />
            <Button title="Sign in" onPress={() => void signIn()} />
          </View>
        </>
      ) : null}
      {principal.status === 'authenticated'
        ? <Button title="Sign out" onPress={() => void signOut()} />
        : null}
      {recoveryCodes ? (
        <View>
          <Text style={styles.recoveryTitle}>
            Save these recovery codes now. They are shown once.
          </Text>
          <Text selectable style={styles.recoveryCodes}>{recoveryCodes.join('\n')}</Text>
        </View>
      ) : null}
    </View>
  );
}

const snapshotEnvFiles = (directory) => {
  const files = {};
  const visit = (current, prefix = '') => {
    const entries = readdirSync(current, { withFileTypes: true })
      .sort((left, right) => left.name.localeCompare(right.name));
    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (entry.name === 'node_modules' || entry.name === '.git') continue;
      const path = join(current, entry.name);
      const relativePath = join(prefix, entry.name);
      if (entry.isDirectory()) visit(path, relativePath);
      else if (/^\.env/u.test(entry.name)) files[relativePath] = readFileSync(path).toString('base64');
    }
  };
  visit(directory);
  return files;
};

// @ref LLP 0223#design-detail — the Expo starter keeps the zero-config
// assertion and app-level round trip visible as product evidence. The shared
// runner supplies its bound step and cleanup envelope, not the product claim.
async function runZeroConfigSupervisedConnect({ stateRoot, signal }) {
  const supervisedReadyFile = join(stateRoot, 'supervised.ready.json');
  const supervisedDatabase = join(stateRoot, 'supervised.sqlite3');
  const supervisorDescriptor = join(stateRoot, 'expo-supervisor.json');
  const metroScript = join(stateRoot, 'headless-metro.mjs');
  const environmentBefore = snapshotEnvFiles(root);
  const events = [];
  writeFileSync(metroScript, `
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

const port = Number(process.env.SNAPBACK_EXPO_METRO_PORT);
const supervisorOrigin = process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_SNAPBACK_SUPERVISOR_ORIGIN;
const server = createServer((_request, response) => {
  response.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json');
  response.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, supervisorOrigin }));
});
server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1');
const stop = () => server.close(() => process.exit(0));
process.once('SIGTERM', stop);
process.once('SIGINT', stop);
`);

  let supervisor = null;
  let roundTripBoot = null;
  let details = null;
  try {
    supervisor = await runExpoDev({
      backendDirectory: join(root, 'snapback'),
      projectRoot: root,
      expoDirectory: root,
      readyFile: supervisedReadyFile,
      database: supervisedDatabase,
      platform: 'ios',
      email: 'zero-config@expo-chat.test',
      metroCommand: { command: process.execPath, args: [metroScript] },
      serverStdio: ['ignore', 'ignore', 'ignore'],
      signal,
      onEvent(event) { events.push(event); },
    });
    assert.equal(supervisor.state, 'ready');
    assert.equal(supervisor.connectCarrier, 'supervisor-rendezvous');
    const readiness = events.find((event) => event.state === 'ready');
    assert(readiness, 'supervised acceptance must observe the final readiness event');
    assert.equal(readiness.connectCarrier, 'supervisor-rendezvous');
    assert.equal(readiness.authority.status, 'ready');
    assert.equal(readiness.authority.authMode, 'sessions');
    assert.deepEqual(snapshotEnvFiles(root), environmentBefore);
    assert.equal(existsSync(supervisorDescriptor), true);
    assert.equal(statSync(supervisorDescriptor).mode & 0o777, 0o600);

    const metroResponse = await fetch(supervisor.metroOrigin, { signal });
    assert.equal(metroResponse.ok, true);
    const metroFacts = await metroResponse.json();
    assert.equal(metroFacts.supervisorOrigin, readiness.bootstrap.origin);

    const environment = createSupervisedExpoEnvironment({
      exchangeOrigin: readiness.bootstrap.origin,
      bindingCache: null,
      appState: {
        currentState: 'active',
        addEventListener() { return { remove() {} }; },
      },
    });
    roundTripBoot = createSnapbackExpoBoot({ app, environment });
    const bootState = await roundTripBoot.start();
    assert.equal(bootState.status, 'ready');
    assert.equal(bootState.binding.source, 'supervised-dev');
    assert.equal(bootState.binding.target.origin, readiness.binding.target.origin);
    const roundTripClient = roundTripBoot.appClient().client;
    const before = (await roundTripClient.query(api.messagesForConversation, {
      args: { conversationId: CONVERSATION_ID },
    })).rows;
    const body = `Zero-config supervised acceptance ${process.pid}`;
    const mutation = await roundTripClient.mutate(api.sendMessage, {
      args: {
        conversationId: CONVERSATION_ID,
        senderId: 'user_ada',
        body,
      },
      clientMutationId: `zero-config-supervised-${process.pid}`,
    });
    assert.equal(typeof mutation.result, 'string');
    const after = (await roundTripClient.query(api.messagesForConversation, {
      args: { conversationId: CONVERSATION_ID },
    })).rows;
    assert.equal(before.some((row) => row.text === body), false);
    assert(after.some((row) => row._id === mutation.result && row.text === body));
    details = {
      connectCarrier: readiness.connectCarrier,
      authMode: readiness.authority.authMode,
      queryFunctionId: api.messagesForConversation.id,
      mutationFunctionId: api.sendMessage.id,
      descriptorMode: '0600',
    };
  } finally {
    await roundTripBoot?.dispose();
    await supervisor?.close();
  }
  assert.deepEqual(snapshotEnvFiles(root), environmentBefore);
  assert.equal(existsSync(supervisorDescriptor), false);
  return details;
}

export const entityByExternalId = defineJsLiveQuery({
  args: { kind: v.string(), externalId: v.string() },
  auth: 'authenticated',
  reads: ['users', 'posts', 'conversations', 'messages'],
  result: results.records(v.object({ id: v.string() }), { minItems: 0, maxItems: 1 }),
  handler: async (ctx, args) => {
    await requireCurrentUser(ctx);
    let row = null;
    if (args.kind === 'user') row = await ctx.db.query('users').withIndex('by_handle').eq('handle', normalizeHandle(args.externalId)).first();
    if (args.kind === 'post') row = await ctx.db.query('posts').withIndex('by_external_id').eq('externalId', args.externalId).first();
    if (args.kind === 'conversation') row = await ctx.db.query('conversations').withIndex('by_external_id').eq('externalId', args.externalId).first();
    if (args.kind === 'message') row = await ctx.db.query('messages').withIndex('by_external_id').eq('externalId', args.externalId).first();
    return row ? [{ id: row._id }] : [];
  },
});

export const starterCounts = defineJsLiveQuery({
  args: {},
  auth: 'authenticated',
  reads: ['users', 'follows', 'posts', 'likes', 'reposts', 'conversations', 'memberships', 'messages', 'receipts'],
  refusals: ['PROFILE_REQUIRED'],
  result: results.records(v.object({

    follows: v.integer(),

    conversations: v.integer(),
    memberships: v.integer(),

    receipts: v.integer(),
  }), { minItems: 1, maxItems: 1 }),
  handler: async (ctx) => {

only.** This page describes the local dev/test target.\n> Hosted targets make deliberately weaker or different claims — see\n> [auth/targets](./targets.md).\n\nPassword login is a credential class on the ordinary\n[sessions surface](./sessions-and-principals.md). A successful signin runs the\nsame session-creation core as an email-code exchange and returns the same\ncredential response. There is **no parallel identity system, no parallel token,\nand no separate session shape** — one principal, several credentials.\n\nThis is the first sign-in method a browser app can offer end users without a\nmail adapter. Email-code login still has no self-serve production path (no\ndelivery), so if you need a real user to sign themselves in today, this is it.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.21 -->\n## Declare email identifiers before activation\n\nChoose the password identifier in the app's `defineAuth` program and pass that\nprogram to `defineSchema(..., { auth: { mode: 'sessions' }, authProgram })`.\nUse `identifier: 'email'` for the email-v1 canonicalizer:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/snapback/schema.mjs\nconst authProgram = defineAuth({\n  version: 1,\n  mechanisms: {\n    password: {\n      kind: 'password',\n      identifier: 'email',\n      provider: 'builtIn',\n      recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n    },\n  },\n  assuranceRequirements: {},\n  recoveryPolicy: {\n    recoveryCodes: {\n      enabled: true,\n      requiredWhen: 'no-independent-recovery',\n      rotateAfterUse: true,\n      plaintextCustody: 'one-time-response',\n    },\n    lastAuthenticator: 'enforce',\n  },\n  guestPolicy: { enabled: false },\n  secretReferences: {},\n});\n```\n\nCodegen derives the non-secret `app.authBootstrap` policy from that normalized\nauth program and adds `auth.application-bootstrap.v1` to the generated app's\nrequired capabilities. Do not hand-author either fact. Binding admission\nintersects the generated password mechanism with the target's\n`auth.passwords` capability before credential UI can issue network work. The\nReact template's static acceptance check pins both generated facts:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/acceptance.static.mjs\nassert.equal(descriptor.authBootstrap.format, 'snapback.application-auth-bootstrap.v1');\nassert(descriptor.capabilities.required.includes('auth.application-bootstrap.v1'));\n```\n\n`identifier: 'username'` selects username-v1. An app with no declared password\nmechanism keeps the existing username-v1 default. The choice is stored in\ncatalog v4 at the first sessions activation and is immutable afterward;\ncodegen/startup refuses a later contradictory declaration with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_IDENTIFIER_MODE_IMMUTABLE` instead of reinterpreting\nexisting identities.\n\nThe default password minimum is 12 decoded UTF-8 bytes. To choose a different\napp-wide minimum, set `minimumLength` on the password mechanism:\n\n```js fragment reason=\"policy-only excerpt from the defineAuth password mechanism shown above\"\npassword: {\n  kind: 'password',\n  identifier: 'email',\n  provider: 'builtIn',\n  recovery: 'recoveryCodes',\n  minimumLength: 8,\n}\n```\n\nThe declaration is a safe integer from 8 through 128; every password\nmechanism in one program must resolve to the same value or codegen refuses\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_CONFLICT`. The maximum remains 1,024\nUTF-8 bytes, and common-password screening still applies. Omit the field to\nkeep 12. This is a startup policy, so restart the backend after changing it. An\ninvalid declaration refuses codegen/startup with\n`SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_MINIMUM_LENGTH_INVALID`; an entered password that\nmisses the active policy refuses with `SNAPBACK_AUTH_PASSWORD_POLICY`, whose\nredacted details name the active minimum, maximum, default, and `defineAuth\nmechanisms.<name>.minimumLength` configuration path.\n\n<!-- since: 0.1.23 -->\n## Sign up, then sign in\n\n> **One application client owner is one custody context.** In a Node\n> acceptance process, constructing multiple clients without an explicit\n> `storagePartition` can make personas share login: the second client adopts\n> the authenticated durable default owner and can have the same user. Use one\n> stable partition per persona/worker from the\n> [multi-persona client recipe](../recipes/multi-persona-clients.md).\n\nFor an ordinary React application, construct one application client from the\ngenerated `app` and the admitted environment binding, then give that owner to\n`SnapbackProvider`. The clean browser Explicit fixture is runnable first-party\nsource; its host supplies the admitted binding and platform:\n\n```js source=tests/fixtures/application-auth/browser-explicit/application/App.mjs\nimport React from 'react';\nimport { createSnapbackAppClient } from '@expo/snapback-client';\nimport {\n  SnapbackProvider,\n  useSnapbackAuth,\n  useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal,\n} from '@expo/snapback-react';\n\nimport { app } from './snapback/generated/app.mjs';\nimport { createAuthPanel } from '../../shared/auth-panel.mjs';\n\nconst AuthPanel = createAuthPanel({\n  useAuth: useSnapbackAuth,\n  useCurrentPrincipal: useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal,\n});\n\nexport async function createApplication({ binding, platform, now, onSnapshot }) {\n  const appClient = await createSnapbackAppClient({ app, binding, platform, now });\n  return Object.freeze({\n    app,\n    appClient,\n    element: React.createElement(\n      SnapbackProvider,\n      {\n        appClient,\n        fallback: (state) => React.createElement(\n          'pre',\n          { 'data-fixture': 'boot' },\n          JSON.stringify(state),\n        ),\n      },\n      React.createElement(AuthPanel, { onSnapshot }),\n    ),\n  });\n}\n\nexport { app };\n```\n\n`fallback` owns construction states. When children render, the bootstrap is\n`ready`: binding, custody, client, and authority synchronization have settled.\n`ready` does **not** mean signed in. A cold password-only app still settles a\nserver-witnessed anonymous principal so the entry form is reachable; generated\n`anonymousPublic` controls anonymous app-data access, not whether boot can\nfinish.\n\nInside the provider, use the canonical facade and principal projection. The\ntemplate clears any previous recovery projection before every operation, then\nkeeps the signup result only long enough to render its one-time codes:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/src/App.tsx\nexport function App() {\n  const auth = useSnapbackAuth();\n  const principal = useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal();\n  const workspace = useSnapbackQueries(workspaceQueries);\n  const createTodo = useSnapbackMutation(api.createTodo);\n  const connection = useSnapbackConnection();\n  const [email, setEmail] = useState('person@example.com');\n  const [password, setPassword] = useState('replace-this-password');\n  const [recoveryCodes, setRecoveryCodes] = useState<readonly string[] | null>(null);\n  const todos = workspace.queries.todos.status === 'ready'\n    || workspace.queries.todos.status === 'refreshing'\n    ? workspace.queries.todos.data\n    : [];\n\n  const signUp = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    const result = await auth.signUpWithPassword({ email, password });\n    setRecoveryCodes(result.recoveryCodes);\n  };\n  const signIn = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    await auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });\n  };\n  const signOut = async () => {\n    setRecoveryCodes(null);\n    await auth.signOut();\n  };\n```\n\nRender all five `CurrentPrincipalSnapshot` states distinctly: `loading`,\n`anonymous`, `authenticated`, `refreshing`, and `blocked`. Only the\n`authenticated` arm has a current `userId`. The template's account UI also\nmakes the recovery handoff explicit:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/react/src/App.tsx\n        {recoveryCodes ? (\n          <aside>\n            <strong>Save these recovery codes now. They are shown once.</strong>\n            <pre>{recoveryCodes.join('\\n')}</pre>\n          </aside>\n        ) : null}\n```\n\nThe application must hand those codes to the user for separate safe custody\nat signup. They are not session credentials: do not put them in the app\nclient, general persistence, logs, analytics, diagnostics, or a later account\nscreen. Snapback cannot read them back. Clear the projection when the user\nleaves the handoff or starts another auth action. Recovery consumption and\nrotation each return a new one-time set and require the same handling; see\n[Recovery codes are the recovery path](#recovery-codes-are-the-recovery-path).\n\nThe complete ordinary sequence is:\n\n1. Wait for provider `ready`; `useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal()` reports the\n   settled anonymous arm.\n2. Call `auth.signUpWithPassword`. Save the returned recovery codes now; the\n   principal projection becomes `authenticated` only after coordinator\n   adoption and its barrier settle.\n3. On a full browser reload, construct the same app client again. Browser and\n   Expo web use IndexedDB plus Web Locks, so the owner restores the settled\n   principal without another signup or sign-in. `dispose()` only releases the\n   process projection; it does not sign out or delete durable custody.\n4. Call `auth.signOut()`. The provider blanks predecessor protected state,\n   revokes the session, settles anonymous custody, and only then publishes the\n   anonymous principal.\n5. Call `auth.signInWithPassword` for the existing account. Sign-in returns\n   the ordinary credential projection, not recovery codes.\n6. To switch users, sign out first, replace the form identity, then sign in or\n   sign up. Entry while an application-entered or restored principal is still\n   authenticated refuses with a typed `signOut` remediation; there is no\n   implicit latest-user-wins switch.\n\nThe browser restoration path is package-tested against a fresh application\nclient over the same durable custody record:\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-client/app-client.test.mjs\n    restored = await createSnapbackAppClient(input);\n    assert.equal(restored.auth.currentPrincipal().status, 'authenticated');\n    assert.equal(\n      restored.auth.currentPrincipal().provider,\n      null,\n      'restoration does not fabricate the provider availability key as issuance provenance',\n    );\n    assert.equal(restored.bootstrapState().authoritySource, 'durable-restored');\n```\n\n### Use the same owner through Expo\n\nAn Expo application passes only the generated `app` to the ordinary provider.\nWhen that descriptor carries the generated bootstrap policy and required\ncapability, `SnapbackExpoProvider` resolves the environment and delegates to\nthe same application-client owner; its `useSnapbackAuth` and\n`useSnapbackCurrentPrincipal` exports project the same contracts. The current\n`expo-chat` template keeps this composition at the root:\n\n```tsx source=packages/snapback-cli/templates/expo-chat/App.tsx\nexport default function App() {\n  const [thread, setThread] = useState<Thread | null>(null);\n  return (\n    <SnapbackExpoProvider app={app} fallback={(state: ExpoBootState) => <BootFallback state={state} />}>\n      <TestPersonaProvider>\n        <AccountEntry />\n        {thread\n          ? <ChatScreen conversationId={thread.id} title={thread.title} onBack={() => setThread(null)} />\n          : <InboxScreen onOpen={(id, title) => setThread({ id, title })} />}\n      </TestPersonaProvider>\n    </SnapbackExpoProvider>\n  );\n}\n```\n\n**Expo web** selects the shipped browser IndexedDB/Web Locks carrier and has\nthe same durable reload restoration as React web. **Both native OS paths ship\nat the exact iOS/Android + `single-runtime` tuples in the published 0.1.24\nclosure** (first publish recorded in\n[the closed custody first-publish gate](repo:issues/closed/20260816-custody-first-publish-gate.md));\nneither path falls back to memory. The iOS receipt proves only the share-sheet extension kind. Its\nbuilt/embedded Notification Service Extension remains a nonclaim because\nsimulator `simctl push` cannot invoke that service stage. The disposable\ncross-platform `expo-chat` template\ntherefore keeps `custody: 'volatile-explicit'`: it can exercise\nsignup/sign-in/sign-out but cannot claim process-death restoration or supported\nrelaunch. Read [Authenticate a native app](./native-apps.md) for the native\nbroker and custody threat boundary, and [Targets](./targets.md) before making\nany hosted or production claim.\n\n### Keep custom identity brokers on the advanced seam\n\nIf the app already has an external identity front door, custom gateway, or\napplication-owned identity binding, keep that explicit composition on the\n[browser sign-in and reload custody recipe](../recipes/browser-auth.md). That\nrecipe deliberately owns a trusted broker, `AuthCoordinator`, and one-use\nexchange; it is not a second spelling for the first-party password journey.\nThe ordinary and advanced owners cannot share one app/storage partition.\n\n### Use the low-level methods only in advanced compositions\n\nThe underlying client methods remain available for custom shells and tests.\n`authPasswordSignup` mints an ordinary session and adopts it into an\napplication-supplied `AuthCoordinator`, exactly as `authExchange` does. You\nneed no admin token, no impersonation capability, and no `auth.mintSession`.\n\n```js source=packages/snapback-client/password-auth.test.mjs\n    const result = await fixture.client.authPasswordSignup({\n      email: 'person@example.com',\n      password: PASSWORD,\n    });\n    assert.equal(result.session.userId, USER);\n    assert.equal(fixture.coordinator.authority.userId, USER);\n    assert.equal(Object.hasOwn(result, 'token'), false);\n```\n\n`authPasswordSignIn` takes the same `{ email, password }` and returns the same\nshape. After either, the client holds an ordinary session: protected queries,\nrefresh, the logout barrier, and reload restoration all behave exactly as they\ndo after an email-code exchange.\n\nBoth methods require an `AuthCoordinator` and an anonymous predecessor — they\ncreate a fresh authority, so they adopt through the same anonymous-issuance\npath `authExchange` uses. The bearer is never returned to your code; the\ncoordinator owns it. An ordinary React or Expo app should not construct that\ncoordinator itself; use the application-client/provider journey above.\n\n## The exact session shape\n\nTwo different shapes carry the user id, at two layers. Both are real; use the\none for the layer you are at.\n\n**On the wire**, `POST /auth/password/signin` returns the LLP 0057 composed\ncredential response — the same five fields as `/auth/exchange`:\n\n```text\n{\n  \"tokenType\": \"Bearer\",\n  \"token\": \"…\",\n  \"refreshAfter\": 604800000,\n  \"session\": {\n    \"id\": \"…\",\n    \"userId\": \"usr_…\",          ← the server-issued principal\n    \"provider\": \"local-password\",\n    \"createdAt\": 0,\n    \"expiresAt\": 0,\n    \"absoluteExpiresAt\": 0\n  },\n  \"authorityDescriptor\": { \"descriptorVersion\": 1, \"authorityInstanceId\": \"aut_…\", \"sessionGeneration\": 1 }\n}\n```\n\n**In the client**, the session projection nests authority, and\n`session.authority.userId` is the principal:\n\n```text\nsession.authority.userId        ← principal id, client-side projection\nsession.authority.isAuthenticated\ncredential.session.userId       ← the same principal, wire response\n```\n\n`session.provider` reports `local-password` at mint **and on every later\nrefresh**, so a session's credential class stays legible for its whole life.\n\nSignup additionally returns `recoveryCodes` — the only response that carries a\nsixth field. Everything else stays byte-shape-identical to `/auth/exchange`.\n\n## Recovery codes are the recovery path\n\nSignup returns eight one-time recovery codes. **They are shown exactly once**\nand are not readable again — not through the admin console, not through any\nroute. Store them at signup or lose them.\n\n- `authRecoveryConsume({ email, code })` mints a session and automatically\n  replaces the whole set. A consumed code cannot be reused.\n- `authRecoveryRotate()` replaces the set for an authenticated principal —\n  use it after suspected disclosure.\n\nRecovery codes never enter coordinator custody, the public credential\nprojection, or error diagnostics.\n\n## Changing a password\n\n`authPasswordChange({ currentPassword, newPassword })` requires both an\nauthenticated session **and** the current password — a stolen bearer alone\ncannot rotate a credential.\n\nChange is a **same-authority rotation**, not a new login: it rotates the acting\nsession's bearer, keeps the authority instance id, and revokes the user's\n*other* sessions. A session belonging to a different user is untouched. Because\nthe authority is preserved, the client adopts it through the same rotation path\nrefresh uses.\n\n`authPasswordSet({ newPassword, stepUp })` adds a first password to a principal\nthat has none. import { Stack } from 'expo-router';

import { registerExpoFileSystemRqsFiles } from '@expo/snapback-client';
import { SnapbackExpoProvider } from '@expo/snapback-expo';
import type { ExpoBootState } from '@expo/snapback-expo';

import { app } from '../snapback/generated/app.mjs';
import { AuthBoundary } from '../src/auth-boundary';
import { palette } from '../src/ui';

if (Platform.OS !== 'web') registerExpoFileSystemRqsFiles(FileSystem, { crypto: Crypto });

function BootFallback({ state }: Readonly<{ state: ExpoBootState }>) {
  const diagnostic = 'diagnostic' in state ? state.diagnostic : null;
  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={styles.fallback}>
      <Text style={styles.title}>{state.status === 'starting' ? 'Opening Clique…' : "Clique couldn't start"}</Text>
      {diagnostic ? <Text style={styles.error}>{diagnostic.code}: {diagnostic.message}</Text> : null}
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

export default function RootLayout() {
  return (
    <SnapbackExpoProvider app={app} fallback={(state: ExpoBootState) => <BootFallback state={state} />}>
      <AuthBoundary>
        <Stack screenOptions={{ headerStyle: { backgroundColor: palette.background }, headerTintColor: palette.text }}>
          <Stack.Screen name="index" options={{ headerShown: false }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="profile/[handle]" options={{ title: 'Profile' }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="profile/edit" options={{ title: 'Edit profile' }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="thread/[id]" options={{ title: 'Thread' }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="chats" options={{ title: 'Chats' }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="conversation/[id]" options={{ title: 'Conversation' }} />
          <Stack.Screen name="settings" options={{ title: 'Settings' }} />
        </Stack>
      </AuthBoundary>
    </SnapbackExpoProvider>
  );
}

  fallback: { alignItems: 'center', backgroundColor: palette.background, flex: 1, justifyContent: 'center', padding: 24 },
  title: { color: palette.text, fontSize: 24, fontWeight: '800' },
  error: { color: palette.danger, marginTop: 12 },
});

# diary.md — lane opus-clique-explicit (Clique on Snapback 0.1.25, explicit profile)

## M1 — accounts and profiles

### What I built

- A Snapback backend in the **default explicit profile**: `snapback/schema.mjs`
  with a `defineAuth` program (password credentials on the built-in provider,
  `minimumLength: 8`, no guest arm, no email-code arm) and eleven tables;
  `snapback/functions.mjs` with `defineJsLiveQuery` / `defineJsMutation` /
  `defineAssetUpload` declarations and generated exact function references
  under `snapback/generated/`.

  `src/social-ui/`), with a persistent nav rail (feed tabs + chats list) and a
  routed main column, so the contract's `sm-feed-tab-*` and `sm-chats-item`

  `starter-m1.log` through the app's real signup and mutation paths — ~1,000
  password hashes is the M6 shape; here it is 8 — plus a `seedRefs` ledger
  table so a second run of the same segment is a no-op.
- A one-command acceptance suite (`npm run acceptance -- --milestone m1`)
  that seeds, runs the milestone's suite-required assertions against the real
  web client, validates a coverage manifest against the instrument's
  `assertions.json`, and writes the suite receipt, the choreography
  suite-status linkage, and the typed D0.6 observation sidecar.

### What felt easy

- **Codegen diagnostics are unusually good.** Every refusal named its rule, a
  source span, an admitted alternative, and a build-bound guide anchor. When
  the inline handler profile rejected `obj[key]`, the message told me the exact
  rule (`inline.syntax.forbidden`), the exact line, and the page to read. I
  never had to guess.
- **The served Guide is a real product.** `snapback guide <query>` plus
  `GET /_snapback/guide/<page>.md` off the running binary meant documentation
  was build-bound to the binary I was actually running, and section flats let
  me pull "backend" and "clients" once instead of grepping a wiki.
- **Password auth is genuinely built in.** `defineAuth` + `signUpWithPassword`
  / `signInWithPassword` / `signOut` gave me M1's whole auth surface — server
  hashing, one-time recovery codes, server-side logout revocation — without me
  writing a KDF or a session table. That is the single biggest hour saved.
- **Live queries are the default shape.** `profileByHandle` is thirty lines of
  declaration and the other client saw a profile edit in ~300 ms with no
  subscription plumbing on my side.

### What fought me

- **Random ports in the paved dev loop.** `snapback dev --expo` picks free
  loopback ports for Metro's front proxy and the supervisor bootstrap origin,
  which collides with this lane's fixed 42160–42179 constraint. I ended up
  running the backend with `--external-client-origin` and hand-building the
  `supervised-dev` AppBindingV1 in `src/backend.tsx`. That took reading
  `app-client.mjs` to learn that the binding's `capabilities.offered` must
  include `auth.passwords`, which no page states.
- **`custody: 'volatile-explicit'`.** The expo-chat template ships it, AGENTS.md
  tells you not to move off it, and it silently selects *memory* auth custody —
  so the session does not survive a reload, which is M1 acceptance item 3. The
  guide text says Expo web "has the same durable reload restoration as React
  web", which is true only under `durable-required`. I had to read
  `app-client.mjs` to find the selector.
- **Inline handler admission.** Computed member access and top-level `const`
  capture are both refused. My first `functions.mjs` used plain objects as maps
  everywhere; converting to `Map`/`Set` was mechanical but unexpected, and the
  rule is a page I had not been routed to by the start packet.
- **A two-step signup.** Snapback owns the principal; my app owns the profile
  row with the unique handle. That makes "duplicate handle is rejected with a
  visible error" a two-server-step story: a public pre-check query, then the
  unique index as the real authority. It works and it is honest, but it is more
  ceremony than a single `createUser({handle})`.

### What the explicit profile saved or cost

- **Saved:** every function is a value I can read. `results.records(v.object({…}))`
  made the wire contract of each screen explicit, and the generated
  `api.d.ts` typed the client without me writing a single interface twice. The
  `refusals: [...]` + `ctx.refuse(code)` channel is the thing I miss most in
  other backends: `HANDLE_TAKEN` arrives at the browser as a stable code, not a
  message I have to regex.
- **Cost:** the declaration is verbose and the handler dialect is a subset of
  JavaScript. `Object.keys(map).map(k => map[k])` is not admissible; neither is
  a shared `const MAX_ROWS`. I paid maybe 25 minutes to that dialect. The
  `authScopeField` declaration also refused my computed-record field name
  (`FUNCTION_UNKNOWN_FIELD` — it must name a *table* field), so principal-scoped
  handler queries currently carry no scope declaration at all.

### What documentation or diagnostic was missing

1. **No page tells you which capabilities a hand-built AppBinding must offer.**
   `auth.passwords` is only discoverable by reading
   `@expo/snapback-client/app-client.mjs`. A "run Expo against a fixed-port
   backend" recipe would have saved the whole detour.
2. **`custody` is documented as a posture, not as a mechanism.** Nothing says
   "volatile-explicit means memory custody, so reload loses the session."
3. **`authScopeField` on handler-backed live queries.** The guide describes it
   as declaring "which result field represents the principal", but codegen
   validates it against the primary table's fields. Either the prose or the
   validator is wrong; with a computed record contract there is no way to
   declare it at all.
4. **The instrument's choreography cannot install its own dependencies** when
   the instrument tree is read-only; a lane-side resolver shim was needed. That
   is an instrument-packaging gap, not a Snapback one.

### M1 result

Suite 7/7 suite-required assertions, coverage 7/7. Choreography segment `m1`
3/3 required assertions passed, `green: true`, `nonGreenCause: null`.

A group messaging and social app (accounts, profiles, a follow graph, post

| Path | What it is |

| `snapback/functions.mjs` | Live queries, mutations, and asset upload intents |

Two servers, both inside this lane's pinned port range:

# 2. Expo web client (port 42161)

One documented command per milestone, from a clean checkout against the running
backend and web client:

Each run:

1. installs that milestone's fixture action-log segments through the app's own

3. validates a coverage manifest — every suite-required assertion must map to a

# Building Clique on Snapback — a comparison with backends I know

*Written after M1–M3 of the `social-messenger` brief, before any numbers were
tallied. Lane `opus-clique-explicit`; Snapback 0.1.25, default explicit
authoring profile; Expo Router web client on the frozen UI kit.*

---

## The shape of the thing

Snapback is not a database with an API bolted on, and it is not a
function-as-a-service with a database attached. It is a **declared application**:
a schema module and a functions module that together compile to an artifact with
a hash, and a running binary that will only serve the artifact you declared. The
first consequence is that there is no "the backend" separate from "my code" — the
generated `api.mjs` I import in React is the same identity the server loaded, and
the client refuses to attach if they disagree. I have never had a stack tell me
"your bundle is one generation ahead of the backend" as a first-class,
recoverable state. Metro handed me exactly that twice and it retried itself.

The second consequence is that everything interesting is a *value in a file*. A
live query is `defineJsLiveQuery({ args, auth, reads, result, handler })`. Its
result contract is `results.records(v.object({...}))`. Its invalidation surface
is the `reads` array. When I wanted to know why my feed was not updating, the
question "what does this query depend on?" had an answer I could read, not a
cache-key convention I had to reconstruct.

## Against Convex

Convex is the closest relative and the comparison is the most interesting.

Convex's `useQuery` is *automatically* reactive: you write a query function, you
call `useQuery`, and reactivity is a property of the whole system. Snapback
splits it — `defineQuery` is callable, `defineLiveQuery` is subscribable, and a
client that subscribes to the wrong one gets `SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_NOT_LIVE` rather
than a silent poll. I liked this more than I expected to. Marking a query live is
a cost decision (a subscription, an invalidation dependency), and Snapback makes
you spend it deliberately. On this app, `feedPage`, `chatMessages`, `myChats`,
and `profileByHandle` are live; nothing else is, and I can see that at a glance.

Where Convex is clearly ahead is the authoring dialect. Convex handlers are
ordinary TypeScript. Snapback's inline handler profile is a **subset**: no
computed member access (`obj[key]`), no captured top-level `const`, no classes,
no imports; same-file `function` declarations are spliced in and everything else
is refused at generation. I rewrote every map in `functions.mjs` as a `Map` and
every membership test as a `Set`. That is maybe half an hour across the whole
build, and the diagnostics are excellent (`SNAPBACK_INLINE_HANDLER_SYNTAX_FORBIDDEN`
with a source span, the admitted alternative, and a guide anchor), but it is a
real tax and it will surprise anyone arriving from Convex.

Where Snapback is clearly ahead of Convex is **auth as a declared program**.
Convex gives you an auth *integration* — you bring Clerk or Auth0 or WorkOS.
Snapback's `defineAuth` gave me email + password with server-side hashing,
one-time recovery codes, server-side logout revocation, and a durable browser
custody carrier, in about forty lines of declaration and no third party. For a
brief that puts OAuth and email delivery explicitly out of scope, that is the
single biggest hour saved in this build. Convex would have had me shipping a
provider integration or hand-rolling argon2id.

The other Snapback advantage over Convex is **declared refusals**. `refusals:
['NOT_ADMIN', 'HANDLE_TAKEN', …]` + `ctx.refuse(code, details)` gives the client
a stable application code that the host will only admit if the function declared
it. My acceptance suite asserts `appCode === 'NOT_ADMIN'` rather than matching a
message. In Convex I would be throwing `ConvexError` with a payload I invented,
which works but is a convention rather than a contract.

## Against Supabase

Supabase's model is Postgres plus RLS plus PostgREST, and the comparison is
mostly about *where the boundary lives*. In Supabase the boundary is the row
policy: the client talks to the table, and the policy decides. Snapback has table
`visibility` too, but the reachable surface is *only the functions you declared*
— there is no generic table endpoint at all. That changes the shape of a security
review. In Supabase I audit policies and then worry about which columns leak
through a `select *`. Here I audit function declarations, and a table nobody
declared a function over is simply unreachable.

I used `public-read` visibility on Clique's tables and put membership scoping in
the query handlers (`chatMessages` returns nothing to a non-member). In Supabase
I would have written that as an RLS policy and gotten defence in depth. That is a
genuine Supabase advantage and I want to be honest that my posture here is
weaker than a policy-backed one would be: Snapback ships a `membership`
visibility kind and I did not use it, because wiring the membership declaration
was more risk than the M1–M3 assertions required. If I were shipping this, that
is the first thing I would go back and do.

Supabase's realtime is also a fair fight and Snapback wins it. Supabase Realtime
gives you row-level change feeds; you still assemble the *view*. Snapback
delivers the query's result — my feed row is a joined, viewer-scoped record with
like counts, repost attribution, and the viewer's own like state, and the client
receives that shape, not four table streams to reduce. Measured on this app, a
new post reached the other browser in ~270 ms end to end with no code of mine in
the path.

Where Supabase is far ahead: **operations and escape hatches**. It is Postgres. I
can open psql. I can write a recursive CTE, a materialized view, a partial index,
a trigger. Snapback's bounded query builder (`.eq/.in/.lt/.gt/.order/.take`) is
deliberately small; `take()` caps at 1,024 rows and refuses an unbounded
`collect()` outright, which is *right* for correctness-at-scale and occasionally
maddening when you know exactly what you want. My "viewer's own likes" projection
is two bounded set reads with an honest 1,024-row ceiling; in Postgres it is a
semi-join and I would not have thought about it.

## Against Firebase

Firebase is the one Clique most resembles in product shape, and the comparison is
lopsided. Firestore's security rules are a separate language with a separate
mental model and a famously bad debugging story; Snapback's authorization is
`auth: 'authenticated'` on the function plus `ctx.auth.userId` in the handler,
and when I got it wrong the failure was a typed refusal, not an empty result set.
Firestore also pushes you toward denormalization because queries cannot join —
which is exactly the trap I fell into anyway when I denormalized follower counts,
and then had to take back. Snapback let me derive those counts at read time
inside the query, and the live invalidation followed the derivation for free.

What Firebase still has that Snapback does not: a hosted production story I can
point a real user at today. Snapback's own guide is scrupulous about this — every
page I read carried a "Local target only" banner and the auth pages say plainly
that there is no production email delivery and no self-serve hosted identity.
That honesty is admirable and it is also a hard limit. Clique runs on my machine.

## Against hand-rolled Postgres + Express

This is the baseline I know best, and it is the comparison where Snapback's value
is easiest to quantify. To reach M1–M3 by hand I would have written: a migration
system, a users/sessions schema, argon2id wiring, a session middleware, a
refresh/rotation story, a logout revocation path, ~25 REST endpoints with
validation, a WebSocket layer, a subscription registry, an invalidation strategy,
an asset upload pipeline with content-type sniffing and EXIF stripping, a
delivery route with caching, and a client cache. Optimistically two weeks. Here
the equivalent is roughly 1,300 lines of `functions.mjs` and 220 lines of
`schema.mjs`, and I spent my actual debugging time on *my own React memoization
bug*, not on any of that infrastructure.

The specific thing I would not get back by hand is the **asset pipeline**. One
`defineAssetUpload` with `delivery: 'public-immutable'` and an image variant, one
`v.assetRef` field, one `ctx.assets.attach` line, and `useSnapbackAssetImage`
rendering the delivery ladder — including holding the placeholder until the
rendition publishes so a plain `<img>` never flashes a 404. Two fixture images
and a playing MP4 with zero URL construction on my side. I have written that
pipeline badly at least twice.

## What actually cost me time

Three things, and none of them were the backend's data model.

1. **A memoization mistake in my own React code** that hid field-only live
   updates while insert/delete updates worked. What made it tractable was that
   Snapback has two client arms: I ran the same live query headlessly, proved the
   server delivered the change in under a second, and knew immediately the bug
   was mine. That two-arm property is underrated as a debugging tool.
2. **Composition at the edges of the paved path.** `snapback dev --expo` picks
   random loopback ports; my lane pins a port range; so I hand-built the
   deployment binding and discovered by reading the published client source that
   it must offer `auth.passwords`. Everything about the binding is validated and
   the diagnostics are precise — but there is no recipe for "Expo against a
   fixed-port backend", and that composition took longer than any schema work.
3. **Dispatch shape and authority fences.** `useSnapbackMutation` returns a
   union; the two variants that resolve a plain result both refuse with
   `SNAPBACK_OUTBOX_AUTHORIZATION_SUSPENDED` while authority is settling. That
   refusal is effect-free and a bounded retry is correct, but I established that
   by reading `@expo/snapback-client`'s source rather than a page.

## The overall impression

Snapback feels like a backend designed by people who have been burned by silent
failure. Almost everything refuses rather than degrades: an unbounded collect
refuses, an undeclared refusal code folds to generic, a mismatched artifact
refuses to attach, a required field cannot be dropped without a migration, a
supervised binding expires. Working inside that is occasionally slow and never
mysterious. The counterweight is that when something *is* mysterious — my stale
rows, the authority-suspended refusal — the observability to diagnose it is not
there yet: `status: ready, freshness: current, connection: live` while serving a
stale row is the one moment in three milestones where the platform told me
nothing useful and I had to build my own instrument.

If I were choosing for a real product with this shape today, I would pick Convex
for the authoring ergonomics if I already had an identity provider, Supabase if I
needed SQL escape hatches or a hosted deployment tomorrow, and Snapback if I
wanted the *whole* app — auth, live queries, presence, assets, offline retention
— to be one declared artifact with one identity and no third parties. On the
strength of M1–M3, the third option is a real option, which is not something I
would have said about a 0.1.x backend going in.
